extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of psychoanalysis, psychology, and humour theory
extracted.subtask_description: Extracting and applying Freud's psychoanalytic criteria for how jokes are produced, structured, and received, including mechanisms of laughter, audience conditions, and joke-techniques. Focus is theoretical analysis of jokes (tendentious and innocent) within a psychoanalytic framework.

rubrics_metrics.name: Subjective motives for joke production
rubrics_metrics.description: The motive force for the production of innocent jokes is not infrequently an ambitious urge to show one’s cleverness, to display oneself; the presence of numerous inhibited instincts, whose suppression has retained a certain degree of instability, will provide the most favourable disposition for the production of tendentious jokes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: obscene jokes may indicate concealed exhibitionism in the inventor; aggressive tendentious jokes succeed best in people with a powerful (inhibited) sadistic component. Use of sexual-constitution components as motives is highlighted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compulsion to communicate the joke
rubrics_metrics.description: No one can be content with having made a joke for himself alone; an urge to tell the joke to someone is inextricably bound up with the joke-work — the psychical process of constructing a joke is not completed until it is communicated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Telling the joke serves to complete the process, provide objective confirmation of success, and to obtain the laughter one cannot generate alone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Third person as decision-maker on joke success
rubrics_metrics.description: In jokes the second (object) person is replaced by a third person — the ‘other’ — who decides whether the joke-work has succeeded; the psychical process in jokes is accomplished between the first person (self) and the third (outside person).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The creator expects the third person to validate the joke; this person’s reaction is integral to the joke’s completion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hearer’s affective state required
rubrics_metrics.description: A person dominated by serious thoughts cannot confirm that a jest has succeeded — the third person must be in a cheerful or at least indifferent state of feeling.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the hearer is hostile, offended, or emotionally engaged in conflicting thoughts, they will respond with indignation rather than laughter; benevolence or neutrality is indispensable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Shared inhibitions between teller and hearer
rubrics_metrics.description: It is essential that the hearer be in psychical accord with the teller, possessing the same internal inhibitions which the joke-work has overcome in the first person.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Laughing at the same jokes signals psychical conformity; each joke calls for a public of its own because the inhibitions to be lifted must be common to audience and teller.

rubrics_metrics.name: Laughter as discharge of cathectic (psychical) energy
rubrics_metrics.description: Laughter arises when a quota of psychical energy previously used for cathexis becomes unusable and finds free discharge; the hearer laughs because inhibitory cathexis is lifted and becomes available for discharge.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Freud adapts Spencer's and other authors' ideas: the hearer’s laughter corresponds to an economy (and then discharge) of inhibition-related expenditure; this explains why the hearer laughs more manifestly than the maker.

rubrics_metrics.name: First person’s inability to laugh: interference with discharge
rubrics_metrics.description: The joke’s creator often cannot laugh because although the inhibitory cathexis has been lifted, there is interference with the possibility of discharge — the liberated energy may be immediately applied to some other endopsychic use or exhaustion by the joke-work itself.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The maker performs expenditure in constructing the joke; that expenditure reduces or diverts the quota available for motor discharge (laughter).

rubrics_metrics.name: Economy vs general relief as sources of pleasure
rubrics_metrics.description: Early 'economy' explanations (saving psychical expenditure) are refined: jokes give pleasure by localized economy but ultimately by relief when saved cathectic energy is prevented from being reused elsewhere and is discharged.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Brief, ‘joking’ economies are pleasurable because they save expected expenditures; ultimate pleasure is from general relief via discharge mediated by the third person.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoidance of conscious intellectual work
rubrics_metrics.description: An awakening of conscious intellectual interest (requiring effort) usually spoils the effect of a joke; allusions must be obvious and omissions easy to fill to avoid demanding intellectual expenditure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Jokes lose effect if the hearer must perform significant intellectual work; this distinguishes jokes from riddles, which demand active problem-solving and therefore usually disrupt laughter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Brevity of expression to minimize attention attack points
rubrics_metrics.description: Jokes try to keep their expression as short as possible so as to offer fewer points of attack to the attention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Short expressions reduce opportunities for attention to interrupt the automatic discharge process; this is 'joking' brevity rather than mere terseness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distraction of attention by structural devices
rubrics_metrics.description: Jokes distract attention by putting forward something in the joke’s form that catches attention (omissions, façades, nonsense) so that liberation and discharge of inhibitory cathexis can be completed without interruption.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Techniques include omissions that invite filling the gaps, nonsense, contradiction, and comic façades; these hold attention in a way that allows the automatic joking process to run.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of omissions and 'fill-in' opportunities
rubrics_metrics.description: Omissions in a joke’s wording offer an incitement to filling up the gaps and thus withdraw attention from the joking process while the discharge occurs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This technique is similar to riddles but used to disengage conscious supervision rather than to demand intellectual resolution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Syllogistic façades and comic façades as auxiliary techniques
rubrics_metrics.description: Syllogistic façades (logical-looking arguments) and comic façades (apparent comic material) serve to hold attention and to provide fore-pleasure that facilitates discharge.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Syllogistic façades set a cognitive task that momentarily occupies attention; comic façades can act as a 'bribing fore-pleasure' enabling the joke-work to proceed automatically.

rubrics_metrics.name: Displacement and representation by the absurd
rubrics_metrics.description: Among joke-techniques, displacement and representation by something absurd both distract attention and intensify effect; displacement disguises the true intention and the absurd captures attention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Displacement should be disguised to hold attention (obvious displacement reveals intentionality and lessens the effect). Examples: witty evasions or answers that anticipate and evade.

rubrics_metrics.name: Novelty/surprise requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: Jokes produce their full effect on the hearer only if they are new and come as a surprise; repetition diminishes effect because attention returns to the memory of the first occasion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This explains short joke-lifespans and the urge to tell jokes to those who have not yet heard them to regain novelty-based pleasure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preventing substitutional (endopsychic) uses of liberated energy
rubrics_metrics.description: It is necessary to guard against the liberated cathectic expenditure finding some other psychical use instead of offering itself for motor discharge; otherwise laughter will not occur.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anything that provokes strong competing thoughts in the hearer will draw liberated energy away from discharge; auxiliary techniques work to minimize this risk.

rubrics_metrics.name: Audience composition and social context constraints
rubrics_metrics.description: The social composition of the audience affects whether a tendentious joke will be received as joke or invective; exposure directed at a respected relative or an audience of the opponent’s friends will meet indignation rather than laughter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Jokes require an audience without factors that provoke opposing feelings; certain settings (e.g., a gathering of priests) preclude specific jokes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comic vs tendentious functions and two-fold aim of technique
rubrics_metrics.description: Joke technique is determined by two purposes: making construction possible in the first person (fore-pleasure, protection from reason) and guaranteeing the greatest pleasurable effect on the third person; elements aimed at gaining pleasure are calculated with an eye to the third person.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Techniques that protect the maker's pleasure (Janus-like character) differ from those that maximize hearer discharge; both are essential for successful jokes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Facetious questions ('Scherzfragen') distinction
rubrics_metrics.description: What are known as 'Scherzfragen' (facetious questions) deviate from jokes because the joking answers they call for cannot be guessed in the same way as allusions or omissions in jokes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although facetious questions can use best techniques (distraction, displacement), they are not 'proper jokes' due to the different cognitive operation required.
